name: Deep Plumbeous
lede: Deep Plumbeous is a cool mid grey from Ridgway's 1912 chart, named for lead, and later picked up again for an industrial RAL signal color.

sections.title: Lead-colored, twice over
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 plate LII gives this hue the name Deep Plumbeous, hue 49′′′′′, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files the nearest category as "grayish blue" in its block 186 [1]. *Plumbeous* means lead-colored, from the Latin *plumbum*; Ridgway built a small family of plumbeous greys across several plates, including the lighter [[slate-grey]] [1]. Our library also places RAL 7046, a later German industrial-signal grey, at an approximate screen match to this same swatch, though the two systems were built decades apart for different purposes [1].

In LCH terms it measures lightness 56, chroma 4, hue 251 degrees, Munsell N 5.5, essentially hueless [1]. Its closest match in the library is [[squirrel-grey]], about 3.2 CIEDE2000 units away, with [[light-violet-grey]] close behind at 3.7 units [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
A match within six CIEDE2000 units covering at least five percent of the canvas turns up in 702 of our 23,781 archive paintings, about 3.0 percent [4]. It peaks in the 1940s, in 5 of 28 paintings, at 6.1 times the overall rate, and is most loved by Bernardo Bellotto, Meindert Hobbema and Albert Marquet, each carrying it in a quarter of their paintings here, more than eight times their own museums' baseline; it most often plays a highlight, in 52 percent of its appearances [4].

The earliest dated match is a folio from a Kalpa-sutra manuscript, 1278, more than six centuries before Ridgway recorded the name in 1912; early centuries are thin in the archive, so this is a floor, not a first, and a photograph of an aged canvas is a screen color, not a pigment test [4].
